Alpha Centauri A.description: Primary of the Alpha Centauri system; a Sol-like star and the anchor of human space.

Alpha Centauri B.description: Orange companion to Alpha Centauri A; its industrial worlds orbit under a dimmer, redder sky.

Alpha Centauri C.description: The red dwarf Proxima; it dominates Proxima's night sky though it lies far from the A–B pair.

Regulus A.description: Fast-rotating blue subgiant at the heart of the Regulus system; Tycho's fierce daylight comes from this star.

Delta Pavonis.description: Quiet G-type subgiant; La Bella Vista orbits under warm, steady light.

61 Virginis.description: Sol-like star hosting Irasia's heavy industry and trade lanes.

61 Ursae Majoris.description: Stable main-sequence star anchoring Tokirev's cold industrial orbit.

18 Scorpii.description: Near-Solar analogue; Fennet grew under its calm temperate light.

Tau Ceti.description: Quiet G dwarf; Fortuna's finance districts orbit a dimmer, steadier sol.

61 Cygni A.description: Orange dwarf of the 61 Cygni binary; New Carthage trades under its ruddy light.

Epsilon Eridani.description: Young K dwarf with elevated particle wind; Horizon's vast cities orbit here.

Wolf 359.description: Dim flare star; Titania IX rides the turbulent skies of its gas-giant primary nearby.

Kepler-35 A.description: Primary of the Kepler-35 circumbinary; Pelagos sees two sols from its sky.

Sirius A.description: Brightest star in Old Earth's night sky; its white light is a familiar marker in the inner systems.

Sirius B.description: Dense white-dwarf companion to Sirius A, a remnant of a once more massive star.

Procyon A.description: Yellow-white subgiant in the Procyon binary, brighter and hotter than the Sol.

Procyon B.description: Compact white-dwarf companion orbiting Procyon A.

Barnard's Star.description: Red dwarf famous for its large proper motion across the Old Earth sky.

Lalande 21185.description: Red dwarf in Ursa Major and one of the closest stellar neighbors to Sol.

Ross 154.description: Active Red dwarf in Sagittarius, known for energetic flares.

Lacaille 9352.description: Red dwarf with a comparatively bright apparent presence for its class.

Kapteyn's Star.description: Old high-velocity red dwarf whose motion marks it as a member of the Galactic halo population.

Groombridge 34 A.description: Red dwarf in a binary system, with a companion separated by a wide orbit.

Luyten's Star.description: Red dwarf in Canis Minor with a long history of astrometric study.

Wolf 1061.description: Red dwarf known to host a compact planetary system.

GJ 15 A.description: Red dwarf in a binary system with a low-mass stellar companion.

YZ Ceti.description: Active red dwarf with a compact planetary system.

LHS 1140.description: Cool red dwarf known for hosting a temperate exoplanet.

TRAPPIST-1.description: Ultra-cool red dwarf famous for its compact system of seven Old Earth-sized planets.

GJ 436.description: Red dwarf hosting a well-studied warm gas giant.

GJ 3470.description: Red dwarf with a low-density Neptune-sized planet.

Epsilon Indi A.description: Orange dwarf in a multiple system, surrounded by a faint stellar and substellar entourage.

Epsilon Indi Ba.description: Brown-dwarf companion to Epsilon Indi A; its spectrum is dominated by molecular absorption.

Epsilon Indi Bb.description: Cooler brown-dwarf companion in the Epsilon Indi system.

61 Cygni B.description: Cooler companion of 61 Cygni A, with deep orange-red light.

40 Eridani A.description: Orange main-sequence primary of a hierarchical triple system.

40 Eridani B.description: White-dwarf companion in the 40 Eridani triple system.

40 Eridani C.description: Red-dwarf outer companion of the 40 Eridani system.

Struve 2398 A.description: Nearby flare-star primary in a binary red-dwarf system.

GJ 887.description: Red dwarf with a relatively high surface temperature for an M star.

GJ 667 C.description: Red-dwarf component of a triple system with several reported planetary signals.

GJ 486.description: Red dwarf hosting a short-period terrestrial planet.

GJ 1214.description: Cool Red dwarf hosting a well-studied small gas giant.

Ross 128.description: Quiet Red dwarf with a known Old Earth-sized planetary companion.

Gliese 876.description: Red dwarf whose planetary system includes multiple giant planets in compact orbits.

Gliese 832.description: Red dwarf with a long-period planetary companion.

Gliese 581.description: Red dwarf made famous by early reports of multiple low-mass planets.

Gliese 667 A.description: K-type primary in the Gliese 667 triple system.

Gliese 667 B.description: Cooler stellar companion to Gliese 667 A.

HD 40307.description: Orange dwarf known for a compact family of detected planets.

HD 85512.description: Orange dwarf with a well-studied planetary candidate from early radial-velocity surveys.

HD 20794.description: Sol-like star with a long history of precision radial-velocity observations.

HD 69830.description: Orange dwarf with a prominent debris disk and several detected planets.

HD 10180.description: Sol-like star with a rich planetary system originally inferred from precision radial velocities.

HD 189733 A.description: Orange dwarf hosting the intensely studied hot gas giant HD 189733 b.

HD 209458.description: Sol-like star hosting one of the first exoplanets observed transiting its star.

51 Pegasi.description: Sol-like star whose hot gas giant companion helped launch the ancient era of exoplanet discovery.

55 Cancri A.description: G-type primary hosting a notably diverse multi-planet system.

47 Ursae Majoris.description: Sol-like star with a long-studied system of giant planets.

Upsilon Andromedae A.description: F-type star with a historically important multi-planet system.

Kepler-35 B.description: Low-mass companion that makes the Kepler-35 system a true binary-star planetary environment.

Kepler-90.description: Sol-like star known for a remarkably large planetary system.

Kepler-11.description: Sol-like star hosting several tightly packed transiting planets.

Kepler-62.description: Cooler orange star with a compact system including two planets in its habitable-zone region.

Kepler-186.description: Red dwarf hosting five known planets, including an Old Earth-sized planet in the temperate zone.

Kepler-452.description: Sol-like star with a well aged planetary system and a well-known transiting rocky super planet.

Kepler-1649.description: Cool red dwarf hosting an Old Earth-sized planet receiving a temperate level of stellar radiation.

Kepler-22.description: Sol-like star with an early-discovered transiting planet in its habitable zone.

TOI-700.description: Cool red dwarf with a compact planetary system containing Earth-sized worlds.

TOI-715.description: Cool red dwarf hosting a transiting planet near the inner edge of its temperate zone.

LHS 475.description: Red dwarf with an Old Earth-sized transiting planet.

LP 791-18.description: Cool red dwarf with a compact planetary system containing a volcanically interesting terrestrial world.

GJ 357.description: Red dwarf with a compact planetary system.

GJ 1132.description: Cool red dwarf whose rocky planet is a target for atmospheric studies.

GJ 9827.description: Orange dwarf hosting several small transiting planets.

K2-18.description: Cool red dwarf hosting a small gas giant in a temperate orbit.

WASP-12.description: Hot, slightly evolved F-type star hosting an extremely irradiated giant planet.

WASP-17.description: Hot F-type star hosting a highly inflated gas giant.

WASP-39.description: Sol-like star whose transiting gas giant has been a major target for atmospheric spectroscopy.

WASP-96.description: Sol-like star hosting a hot gas giant with a well-observed atmosphere.

WASP-121.description: Hot F-type star orbited by an ultra-hot gas giant.

55 Cnc B.description: Faint stellar companion to the 55 Cancri planetary system.

Sol.description: The Old Earth's G-type primary and the historical reference point for human stellar measurements.

Vega.description: Rapidly rotating A-type star and a historic photometric standard, surrounded by a bright debris disk.

Altair.description: Rapidly rotating nearby A-type star whose flattened shape reflects its high spin rate.

Fomalhaut A.description: A-type star encircled by a prominent debris disk.

Arcturus.description: Orange giant and one of the brightest stars visible from Old Earth.

Aldebaran.description: Orange giant marking the eye of Taurus, with a surface far cooler than the Sol.

Betelgeuse.description: Red supergiant in Orion, nearing the end of its stellar evolution.

Rigel.description: Blue supergiant in Orion radiating with enormous luminosity.

Deneb.description: Luminous blue-white supergiant marking the tail of Cygnus.

Antares A.description: Red supergiant at the heart of Scorpius, with a hot blue companion nearby.

Canopus.description: Bright white-yellow supergiant-like giant and the second-brightest star in Old Earth's night sky.

Achernar.description: Rapidly rotating blue star with a strongly oblate shape.

Spica A.description: Hot blue primary in the close Spica binary, a major navigation beacon in Virgo.

Spica B.description: Hot blue companion to Spica A in a tight stellar orbit.

Pollux.description: Orange giant in Gemini and one of the closest evolved stars to Sol.

Castor A.description: White A-type component of the Castor multiple-star system.

Castor B.description: Second bright A-type component of the Castor multiple system.

Capella Aa.description: Cool giant component of the close Capella binary.

Capella Ab.description: Hotter giant companion orbiting Capella Aa.

Polaris Aa.description: Cepheid variable and the primary of the Polaris multiple system.

Regulus B.description: Cool companion to the rapidly rotating Regulus A.

Bellatrix.description: Hot blue giant marking Orion's shoulder.

Alnilam.description: Extremely luminous blue supergiant at the center of Orion's Belt.

Alnitak.description: Hot massive multiple system forming the eastern star of Orion's Belt.

Mintaka A.description: Hot blue primary of the Mintaka multiple system in Orion's Belt.

Mimosa.description: Hot blue giant marking one of the principal points of the Southern Cross.

Hadar A.description: Massive blue giant in a multiple system and a prominent southern-sky star.

Acrux A.description: Hot blue component of the Acrux multiple system at the foot of the Southern Cross.

Shaula.description: Hot blue star in Scorpius, with a close stellar companion.

Alkaid.description: Blue main-sequence star at the end of the Big Dipper's handle.

Mizar A.description: Bright A-type component of the famous visual multiple system in Ursa Major.

Mizar B.description: Companion to Mizar A, forming a celebrated double-star pair.

Alcor.description: A-type companion visually paired with Mizar in Ursa Major.

Eta Carinae A.description: Extremely luminous unstable massive star surrounded by the Homunculus Nebula.

R Doradus.description: Cool red giant with one of the largest stellar disks.

Mira A.description: Pulsating red giant and prototype of the long-period Mira variable stars.

Algol A.description: Hot primary of the eclipsing Algol system, whose brightness changes reveal its orbital geometry.

Algol B.description: Cooler evolved companion of Algol A in the famous eclipsing binary.

Sadr.description: Yellow-white supergiant near the center of the Northern Cross.

82 Eridani.description: A mature G-type dwarf with a little less light than Sol. Its steady output makes 82 Eridani a useful reference point for long-range navigation.

Zeta Eridani.description: A hot A-type binary primary, substantially brighter than Sol. Zeta Eridani is a young, luminous system whose companion makes its stellar neighbourhood more complex than the catalogue entry suggests.

Eta Eridani.description: An evolved K-type giant, swollen to many times the radius of Sol. Its amber light marks a star well beyond the main sequence.

Nu Eridani.description: A massive B-type giant pouring out thousands of times Sol's light. Nu Eridani is a conspicuous beacon, but its intense radiation makes the inner system an unforgiving environment.

Omicron2 Eridani.description: A quiet K-type dwarf with only a fraction of Sol's output. Its low-energy amber light gives the system a markedly different character from the brighter stars of Eridanus.

Gliese 163.description: A dim M-type dwarf whose visible light is only a fraction of a percent of Sol's. Gliese 163 is the sort of low-power primary around which orbital infrastructure must be built close in.

Gliese 180.description: A cool M-type dwarf with an exceptionally low luminosity. Its faint red output concentrates useful stellar energy into a compact inner system.

HD 147513.description: A metal-rich G-type dwarf with a luminosity close to Sol's. HD 147513 is a comparatively familiar-looking primary despite its different place in the stellar map.

HD 128621.description: The catalogue designation for Alpha Centauri B, the cooler companion to Alpha Centauri A. Its orange-gold light comes from a K-type dwarf slightly less massive and luminous than Sol.

HD 134439.description: An old, metal-poor G-type dwarf moving rapidly across the sky. Its chemical composition marks it as a member of the Galaxy's older stellar population.

HD 134440.description: The close companion of HD 134439, another old metal-poor G-type star. The pair's shared motion and unusual chemistry distinguish this otherwise modest system.

Gliese 667 C.description: A cool M-type component of the Gliese 667 triple system. It is by far the faintest of the three stars, but its close planetary architecture has made the system a persistent target of survey work.

HD 101930.description: A cool M-type dwarf with a tiny fraction of Sol's luminosity. HD 101930's weak red output makes its inner system the natural focus of local traffic and settlement.

16 Cygni A.description: A slightly hotter, brighter G-type member of the 16 Cygni binary. Its companion is a similarly Sun-like star, giving the system a rare double-primary character.

16 Cygni B.description: The slightly fainter G-type companion in the 16 Cygni binary. Its long-period giant planet gives the system a particularly interesting outer architecture.

Gliese 777 A.description: A slightly evolved G-type star, brighter than Sol and old enough to have left the simplest main-sequence profile. A faint M-dwarf companion shares the system.

Gliese 777 B.description: A very faint M-type companion to Gliese 777 A. The little red star contributes almost nothing to the system's total light, but is dynamically part of the same stellar neighbourhood.

HD 186408.description: One half of the 16 Cygni-like HD 186408/HD 186427 pair, a solar-type binary separated by a broad stellar orbit. Its G-type spectrum is familiar to human observers.

HD 186427.description: A solar-type companion to HD 186408, slightly brighter and hotter than Sol. The two stars form a wide binary with both components useful as independent stellar references.

HD 190007.description: A cool K-type dwarf radiating at roughly a quarter of Sol's luminosity. Its orange light and modest size give the system a distinctly low-energy profile.

Gliese 806.description: A cool M-type dwarf with very low luminosity. Gliese 806 belongs to the large population of faint red primaries that dominate the local stellar census.

Luyten 726-8 A.description: One of the two extremely faint red dwarfs of the Luyten 726-8 binary. It is an active M-type star whose output is tiny compared with Sol's.

Luyten 726-8 B.description: The companion to Luyten 726-8 A, and one of the faintest stellar primaries in the catalogue. The pair is better known to old navigators as UV Ceti, after the violent flares of component B.

Gliese 1061.description: A very old, very faint M-type dwarf with only a few ten-thousandths of Sol's luminosity. Its compact planetary region is consequently packed close to the star.

HD 2638.description: A G-type dwarf with a luminosity slightly below Sol's. Its planetary system has made this otherwise inconspicuous star a familiar entry in exoplanet catalogues.

HD 11506.description: A slightly hotter and brighter G-type dwarf. HD 11506 hosts a system of giant planets, giving its outer system more structure than its quiet stellar appearance suggests.

Gliese 687.description: A nearby M-type dwarf with a small fraction of Sol's luminosity. Its cool red spectrum and high proper motion are characteristic of the local red-dwarf population.

Gliese 674.description: A low-luminosity M-type dwarf with a compact planetary system. Its close-in worlds orbit in a region that receives the little energy this red star provides.

HD 11964.description: An evolved G-type star somewhat brighter than Sol. Its age and expanded radius place it on the older side of the solar-type stellar population.

70 Virginis.description: An older, slightly evolved G-type star about twice as luminous as Sol. Its giant planet on an eccentric orbit made 70 Virginis one of the early landmarks of the exoplanet era.

109 Virginis.description: A bright F-type main-sequence star, hotter and more luminous than Sol. Its high-energy white light makes it an unmistakable stellar marker in Virgo.

Porrima.description: A close pair of nearly identical F-type stars orbiting one another on a roughly 169-year cycle. From the outer system they resolve into a matched pair of white-gold points.

Vindemiatrix.description: An evolved yellow giant, far larger and more luminous than a main-sequence solar analogue. Vindemiatrix is one of the conspicuous old stars that outline Virgo's traditional star patterns.

Gliese 506.description: A faint M-type dwarf with very little visible output. Its red spectrum is typical of the small, long-lived stars that make up much of the local stellar population.

HD 115617.description: A mature G-type star better known in stellar catalogues as 61 Virginis. It is slightly dimmer than Sol and has a notably low-mass planetary system by giant-planet standards.

Antares.description: The catalogue entry is commonly associated with the red supergiant Antares, a vastly evolved star rather than a dwarf. Its immense radius and intense orange-red light dominate the surrounding system.

HD 159868.description: A solar-type star with a modestly higher luminosity than Sol. Its planetary system includes a long-period giant, making the outer system of greater interest than the quiet primary suggests.

Gliese 682.description: A cool M-type dwarf with a tiny fraction of Sol's luminosity. Its faint red light is characteristic of the low-mass stars that can burn for trillions of years.

Beta Pavonis.description: A luminous A-type star, substantially hotter and brighter than Sol. Beta Pavonis is a clean white stellar beacon against the southern sky.

Gamma Pavonis.description: A relatively quiet G-type dwarf with output close to Sol's. Its modest luminosity and solar-like spectrum make it one of the more familiar southern catalogue stars.

Eta Pavonis.description: A cool, low-mass K-type dwarf with less than half Sol's luminosity. Its amber light marks a substantially cooler stellar environment.

Gliese 411.description: A nearby, high-proper-motion M-type dwarf with a low luminosity. Its motion across the sky is much more noticeable than its faint red light.

Gliese 412A.description: The brighter member of the Gliese 412 binary, a small red dwarf system. Component A is a cool M-type star with very low luminosity.

HD 89744.description: A hot F-type star, brighter and more massive than Sol. HD 89744 is also an unusually active exoplanet host, with a massive planet on a tight orbit.

HD 80606.description: A Sun-like star famous for hosting a giant planet on an exceptionally eccentric orbit. The planet's long, stretched trajectory produces enormous changes in irradiation over its year.

Alioth.description: A hot, luminous A-type star and the brightest member of the Great Bear's central chain. Its white light is considerably stronger than Sol's.

Denebola.description: A young, rapidly rotating A-type star with a prominent debris disk. Denebola's bright white light and dusty surroundings give its system a distinctly active appearance.

Algieba.description: A prominent binary of evolved giant stars in Leo, glowing orange-gold against the darker sky. The combined system is far brighter and more physically extended than a solar-type primary.

Zosma.description: A hot A-type star on the back of Leo's familiar figure. Its white light and relatively high temperature distinguish it from the cooler stars of the constellation.

Gliese 436.description: A cool M-type dwarf hosting a close-in Neptune-mass world. Its faint red light is almost entirely overshadowed by the attention paid to the compact planetary system.

Wolf 424 A.description: One half of the close Wolf 424 red-dwarf binary. Component A is a tiny, faint M-type star whose system is dominated by the dynamics of its companion.

Wolf 424 B.description: The companion to Wolf 424 A, another low-mass M-type dwarf. The pair orbit close enough to form a clearly interacting stellar system at catalogue scales.

Wolf 1055.description: A cool M-type dwarf with very low luminosity. Its small stellar output is concentrated into a compact region of useful orbital space.

Wolf 294.description: A faint red dwarf of the Wolf catalogue, with the low temperature and luminosity typical of late M-type stars.

Wolf 1453.description: Another low-mass red dwarf from the Wolf stellar catalogues. Its faint M-type emission marks a system where useful stellar energy is found only close to the primary.

Kepler-442.description: A cool K-type dwarf known for hosting Kepler-442b, a planet of roughly Earth size receiving moderate stellar energy. The star's orange light is less intense than Sol's.

Fomalhaut.description: A young A-type star surrounded by a broad debris disk and a sharply defined dust ring. Fomalhaut's bright white light and conspicuous disk make the system easy to identify on long-range surveys.

Spica.description: A close, massive blue-white binary whose primary is a rapidly rotating B-type star. The system is extraordinarily luminous and drives a powerful stellar environment.

Dubhe.description: A K-type giant and the primary of a multiple-star system forming the northern edge of the Great Bear's bowl. Its amber light comes from a star far larger than Sol.

Merak.description: A hot A-type star forming one of the two pointer stars of the Great Bear's bowl. Its white light is substantially more luminous than Sol's.

Saiph.description: A massive blue supergiant at the foot of Orion. Saiph's enormous luminosity and strong stellar wind make the inner system a hostile place for conventional infrastructure.

Mintaka.description: A multiple-star system in Orion's Belt, dominated by hot blue-white stars. Its intense ultraviolet output and powerful winds are typical of massive young stars.

Polaris.description: The famous northern pole star, a multiple system whose primary is a yellow supergiant Cepheid variable. Its brightness rises and falls on a regular pulsation cycle.

Groombridge 1830.description: An old, metal-poor G-type subdwarf with unusually high proper motion. Its chemistry and motion mark it as a relic of an older Galactic population.

Ross 614 A.description: A faint red-dwarf primary in a close binary. Its tiny luminosity is typical of low-mass M stars, while the nearby companion gives the system a compact gravitational architecture.

EV Lacertae.description: A small, active M-type flare star. EV Lacertae is prone to powerful stellar outbursts, making radiation forecasts an important part of operating in its inner system.

Teegarden's Star.description: An exceptionally faint M-type dwarf with several confirmed small planets. Its low luminosity keeps the planetary orbits tightly packed around the star.

Gliese 1214.description: A small M-type dwarf hosting a well-studied sub-Neptune. Its planetary system is compact, with the known planet completing an orbit in only a little over a day.

Gliese 649.description: A cool M-type dwarf known to host a long-period giant planet. The contrast between its tiny stellar output and the planet's broad orbit makes the system an interesting navigation marker.

Gliese 710.description: A low-mass K-type star with a long future trajectory through the outer reaches of Sol's neighbourhood. Its high proper motion has made it a familiar object in long-baseline stellar models.

Gliese 849.description: A nearby K-type dwarf hosting a Jupiter-mass planet on a long orbit. Its subdued orange light and wide planetary architecture give the system a quiet outer-system character.

Gliese 370.description: A low-mass K-type dwarf with a fraction of Sol's luminosity. Its orange spectrum is characteristic of stars that remain stable for far longer than Sol.

Gliese 251.description: A cool M-type dwarf with very low luminosity. Gliese 251's known planetary system occupies the close-in orbital region expected around a red primary.

Gliese 205.description: A nearby M-type dwarf with a faint red spectrum and low luminosity. It is a representative member of the abundant local red-dwarf population.

Gliese 59.description: A faint K-type dwarf with a subdued orange spectrum. Its lower mass and luminosity give the system a compact usable orbital region.

Gliese 95.description: A low-luminosity K-type dwarf. Its cool photosphere produces the amber light typical of a star substantially smaller than Sol.

Gliese 117.description: A modest K-type dwarf with less light than Sol. The system's subdued primary makes close orbital operations more practical than in a high-mass stellar system.

Gliese 229 A.description: A nearby M-type dwarf known for its unusually famous companion, the brown dwarf Gliese 229 B. Component A provides only a small fraction of Sol's light.

Gliese 229 B.description: A brown dwarf companion to Gliese 229 A, too cool and faint to sustain hydrogen fusion. It is a substellar object rather than a conventional star, glowing primarily from residual heat.

Gliese 623 A.description: The brighter component of a close red-dwarf binary. Its M-type spectrum and low luminosity make the system's useful orbital zone compact.

Gliese 623 B.description: The smaller companion of Gliese 623 A, a faint M-type dwarf in a close binary configuration.

Gliese 725 A.description: A nearby M-type dwarf and the brighter component of the Gliese 725 binary. Its red light is faint but persistent, characteristic of a long-lived low-mass star.

Gliese 725 B.description: The close M-type companion to Gliese 725 A. Its low luminosity contributes little to the system's total output but gives the binary a distinct double-star signature.

Gliese 783.description: A cool, low-luminosity M-type dwarf. Like many late-type stars, it produces little visible light but can remain on the main sequence for extraordinary lengths of time.

Gliese 785.description: A K-type dwarf with a subdued orange spectrum and roughly half Sol's luminosity. Its stellar environment is cooler and more compact than Sol's.

Gliese 788.description: A faint M-type dwarf with very low luminosity. The system's useful orbital real estate is concentrated close to the primary.

Gliese 793.description: A small red dwarf with low luminosity. Its faint output and cool photosphere place it firmly among the long-lived low-mass stars.

Gliese 797.description: A cool M-type dwarf with a compact stellar environment. Its red emission is weak compared with the familiar G-type primaries of Old Earth's historical records.

Gliese 803.description: A low-mass M-type dwarf with very low luminosity. Its close-in orbital region receives the bulk of the star's available energy.

Gliese 809.description: A faint red M-type dwarf. The star's small mass and low output are typical of the numerous low-energy systems found throughout the local stellar catalogue.

Gliese 820.description: A cool M-type dwarf with low luminosity. Its subdued red spectrum makes it an unremarkable visual beacon but a useful catalogue reference.

Gliese 825.description: A small, faint M-type star. Gliese 825 produces little light compared with Sol, with most useful irradiation confined to close orbital distances.

Gliese 831.description: A cool red dwarf of low luminosity. Its long-lived main-sequence state is typical of stars near the bottom of the stellar mass range.

Gliese 833.description: A faint M-type dwarf with a compact energy envelope. The star's red spectrum is markedly cooler than the G-type light familiar from Sol.

Gliese 835.description: A small M-type primary with very low luminosity. Its system is dominated by close-in orbital space rather than a broad, brightly illuminated outer region.

Gliese 841.description: A cool, faint red dwarf. Gliese 841 is representative of the numerous low-mass stars whose lifetimes vastly exceed those of massive stars.

Gliese 845.description: A low-luminosity M-type star with a compact inner system. Its faint red light gives the primary a distinctly subdued appearance.

Gliese 851.description: A small red dwarf with very low stellar output. Most useful stellar energy in the system is concentrated close to the primary.

Gliese 853.description: A cool M-type dwarf of modest mass and extremely low luminosity. Its system offers little ambient light beyond the inner orbital region.

Gliese 855.description: A faint red dwarf whose low luminosity is characteristic of late-type M stars. Its stellar output is steady on human timescales despite the star's small size.

Gliese 857.description: A low-mass M-type dwarf with a dim red photosphere. It belongs to the numerous class of stars expected to outlive almost every other stellar population.

Gliese 859.description: A small, cool M-type star with very low luminosity. Its compact stellar environment is typical of late red dwarfs.

Gliese 861.description: A faint M-type dwarf with a subdued red spectrum. The star contributes little light to the wider system, but its close-in region remains energetically active.

Gliese 863.description: A low-luminosity red dwarf. Its cool photosphere and small radius place it among the most durable stellar engines in the catalogue.

Gliese 865.description: A faint M-type primary with little visible output. Like other late red dwarfs, it trades brightness for extraordinary longevity.

Gliese 867.description: A compact M-type dwarf with very low luminosity. The system's stellar environment becomes appreciably darker with increasing orbital distance.

Gliese 869.description: A cool red dwarf of the low-mass class. Its weak stellar output makes close orbital placement the defining feature of the system.

Gliese 871.description: A faint M-type star with a compact useful radiation zone. Its low mass places it among the longest-lived conventional stars.

Gliese 873.description: A small red dwarf with very low luminosity. The star's subdued spectrum is typical of late-type stellar systems.

Gliese 875.description: A cool M-type dwarf with little stellar output. Its system is dominated by the close-in orbits where the primary's weak light remains useful.

Gliese 877.description: A faint red dwarf with low luminosity and a cool photosphere. It is a typical low-mass stellar primary rather than a high-energy beacon.

Gliese 879.description: A compact M-type dwarf with very low luminosity. Its red light is weak at range but persistent over stellar timescales.

HD 219134.description: An old K-type dwarf only modestly brighter than the faintest catalogue stars, but with a well-studied system of multiple small planets. Its orange light is significantly cooler than Sol's.

HD 102365.description: A mature, metal-poor G-type dwarf with luminosity close to Sol's. Its old stellar population signature makes it an interesting contrast to younger solar analogues.

HD 10647.description: A bright F-type star with a prominent debris disk. Its planet-hosting system is unusually dusty for a relatively mature star.

HD 20781.description: A quiet K-type dwarf hosting multiple planets. Its cooler spectrum gives the system a warmer, amber cast compared with Sol.

HD 20782.description: A Sun-like star known for a giant planet on an exceptionally eccentric orbit. The planet's stretched path carries it through radically different stellar environments during each revolution.

HD 28185.description: A solar-type star hosting a Jupiter-mass planet on a relatively temperate, near-circular orbit. The outer system is unusually orderly for a giant-planet host.

HD 37124.description: A mature G-type star with a system of multiple giant planets. Its planetary architecture was among the early examples showing that compact multi-planet systems are not unique to Sol.

HD 45364.description: A cool solar-type star with two known giant planets locked near a 3:2 orbital resonance. Their coupled orbits make this system especially distinctive in navigational models.

HD 51608.description: A G-type star hosting multiple planets detected through stellar wobble. Its quiet solar-like spectrum belies a more complicated planetary system.

HD 5319.description: A slightly evolved K-type star with a warm orange spectrum. Its greater radius and luminosity indicate a star beginning to move beyond the main sequence.

HD 134060.description: A metal-poor G-type star hosting two confirmed planets, including a massive close-in world and a more distant companion. The inner planet completes its orbit in only a few days.

HD 136352.description: A nearby G-type star hosting three known planets. Its solar-like spectrum and compact multi-planet architecture make it a useful benchmark system.

HD 142022 A.description: A mature G-type star hosting a long-period giant planet. Its wide planetary orbit gives the system a distinctly outer-system character.

HD 142022 B.description: A faint M-type companion to HD 142022 A. Its tiny contribution to the system's light contrasts sharply with the brighter primary.

HD 14618.description: A cool K-type dwarf with lower luminosity than Sol. Its orange light and modest mass make it a typical long-lived stellar primary.

HD 164595.description: A mature G-type star with a solar-like spectrum. A reported planetary signal made the system briefly notable in SETI circles, although no extraterrestrial transmission was established.

HD 188015.description: A slightly evolved G-type star hosting a giant planet on a broad orbit. Its greater age and luminosity place it beyond the simplest Sol analogue category.

HD 192310.description: A cool K-type dwarf hosting multiple planets. Its orange light and low stellar output produce a compact but well-populated planetary system.

HD 204941.description: A metal-poor, solar-type star with a giant planet on a long-period orbit. Its chemistry marks it as an older member of the Galactic stellar population.

HD 216770.description: A solar-type star hosting a giant planet on an eccentric orbit. The system's planetary dynamics give it more character than the quiet primary suggests.

HD 217107.description: A G-type star with both a close-in giant planet and a much more distant giant companion. The contrast between the two orbits makes HD 217107 a particularly useful planetary reference system.

HD 23079.description: A mature G-type star with a Jupiter-mass planet on an orbit extending well beyond the inner system. A smaller planet has also been reported on a much shorter orbit.

HD 231701.description: A slightly evolved F-type star hosting a giant planet. Its hotter, whiter light and substantial planetary companion distinguish it from the quieter G-dwarf systems nearby.

HD 240237.description: An evolved K-type giant hosting a massive planet. Its swollen stellar radius and amber light indicate a system well past the youthful main-sequence stage.

HD 25015.description: A warm F-type dwarf with a somewhat higher temperature than Sol. Its white-yellow light marks a more energetic stellar environment.

HD 28305.description: An evolved giant star with a high luminosity compared with Sol. Its large radius and orange-yellow spectrum indicate a star late in its normal stellar evolution.

HD 33142.description: An evolved K-type giant hosting planets in its outer system. Its orange light and enlarged radius distinguish it sharply from main-sequence K dwarfs.

HD 34445.description: A mature G-type star with a rich planetary system containing several known planets. Its nearly solar spectrum makes the complexity of the system particularly notable.

HD 38529.description: An evolved G-type star hosting multiple planets, including a massive outer companion. Its enlarged radius and higher luminosity show that the primary is no longer a simple solar analogue.

HD 38858.description: A mature G-type star with a prominent debris disk and a cool, Solar System-like outer architecture. Its spectrum and luminosity make it one of the more familiar-looking stars in the catalogue.

HD 4203.description: A G-type star known for hosting multiple giant planets. Its quiet solar-like primary contrasts with the substantial masses moving through its outer system.

HD 4308.description: A mature, metal-poor G-type star with a confirmed low-mass planet. Its relatively low stellar activity makes the system a useful target for precision measurements.

HD 43691.description: A slightly evolved F-type star hosting a massive planet on a short-period orbit. Its hotter white-yellow light illuminates a comparatively compact planetary system.

HD 45350.description: A G-type star with a giant planet on a long, eccentric orbit. The planet spends much of its cycle far from the primary, giving the outer system an unusually stretched architecture.

HD 47186.description: A solar-type star hosting two planets: a close-in Neptune-mass world and a more distant companion. Their very different orbits make the system an efficient demonstration of planetary diversity.

HD 49674.description: A G-type dwarf with a hot, close-orbiting giant planet. Its primary is modest and solar-like, while the inner planet is subjected to intense stellar irradiation.

HD 50554.description: A slightly hotter F-type star with a giant planet on a broad orbit. Its white light and substantial planetary companion make it a conspicuous exoplanet-system marker.

HD 52265.description: A mature G-type star with a Jupiter-like planet. Its relatively high metallicity and stable output have made it a useful target for precision stellar and planetary studies.

HD 52790.description: A luminous A-type star, much hotter and brighter than Sol. Its strong white light gives the system a very different energy profile from the surrounding G- and K-type stars.

HD 6434.description: An old, metal-poor G-type star hosting a giant planet. Its chemistry and age mark it as a member of an older Galactic stellar population.

HD 65216.description: A G-type star with a planetary system including a giant world on a broad orbit. Its solar-like spectrum makes the outer planetary architecture the dominant point of interest.

HD 66428.description: A mature G-type star with a long-period giant planet. Its quiet primary and distant massive companion give the system a relatively spacious architecture.

HD 68988.description: A G-type star hosting a massive planet on a close orbit. The planet's short year puts it deep inside the system's high-irradiation zone.

HD 72659.description: A mature G-type star with a long-period giant planet. The broad orbit leaves the inner system comparatively open by the standards of early exoplanet discoveries.

HD 73526.description: A G-type star hosting two giant planets in a near-resonant orbital arrangement. Their mutual gravitational interaction gives the system a distinctive dynamical signature.

HD 74156.description: A G-type star with multiple giant planets on substantially different orbits. The system is a classic example of the varied architectures found around solar-type stars.

HD 75289.description: A hot F-type star with a close-in giant planet. The planet's short orbit places it deep in the primary's intense irradiation field.

HD 76700.description: A solar-type star hosting a close-in giant planet. Its compact planetary system contrasts with the broad outer orbits found around many other catalogue stars.

HD 82943.description: A solar-type star hosting multiple giant planets in a dynamically interesting resonant architecture. Its planets have made HD 82943 a standard reference in studies of orbital migration.

HD 83443.description: A cool K-type star with a close-in giant planet. Its orange light is substantially weaker than Sol's, but the inner planet remains strongly irradiated.

HD 86081.description: A hot F-type star hosting a close-in giant planet. Its higher temperature and short planetary orbit combine to make the inner system intensely illuminated.

HD 89345.description: A slightly evolved K-type star with a large radius and a lower-temperature photosphere. Its planet-hosting system orbits a primary already beginning to leave the main sequence.

HD 92788.description: A mature G-type star hosting a massive planet on a broad orbit. Its solar-like light makes the planetary system especially easy to compare with Sol's historical records.

HD 93083.description: A cool K-type star hosting a giant planet. Its subdued orange light and relatively low mass give the system a compact stellar environment.

HD 93722.description: A hot, luminous star with a high-energy spectrum very different from the G-type primaries that dominate human settlement history. Its output makes the inner system a harsh radiation environment.

HD 99109.description: A mature G-type star hosting a long-period giant planet. Its near-solar spectrum gives the system a familiar appearance despite its distinct planetary architecture.
